name: Kotgarhi and Koci, 'Himachali'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hendriksen, Hans. 1986. Himachali Studies III: Grammar. (Det Kongelige Danske Videnskabernes Selskab, Historisk-filosofiske Meddelelser 48,3.) København: Munksgaard. 228 pp.
catalog_locator: pp. 39 and 41 (pp. 49 and 51; p. 40 is the 'Synopsis of stress- and vowel-types' table), chapter 'The Relation between Stress and Vowels' pp. 39-43; supporting: p. 8 stress mark, p. 12 phonemic status of stress and of the high falling tone, pp. 25-26 'Difference of stress', pp. 42-43 position limits, p. 44 tone and stress, p. 67 genetic background
catalog_quote: The vowel /ə/ is never stressed and never occurs in initial or final position in the word. [...] The /ə/ and in certain cases other vowels (see below) will be called empty vowels. The other vowels, which will be called the full vowels, are stressed or unstressed. [...] Only the first sequence vowel, the head vowel, can bear the stress; the sequence is then considered to be stressed. In unstressed sequences none of the vowels are stressed. The term heavy vowel denotes a potentially stressed vowel, i.e. a) a full single vowel, and b) a head vowel. A word cannot contain more than two heavy vowels separated from each other by one or several consonants. [...] Each word which is not enclitic or proclitic has one stress-syllable. If there are two heavy vowels in a word the first bears the stress. This vowel, or, in the case of a head vowel, the sequence which it introduces occurs in non-final position which means that it or the sequence is followed by a consonant. The other heavy vowel, which is unstressed, is final, either alone, if a single vowel, or together with its sequence, if a head-vowel. If there is only one heavy vowel it of course bears the stress. All final morphemes are unstressed.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kotgarhi/Koci word stress is predictable from vowel quality/structure: the reduced 'empty' vowel /ə/ (and in Koci sometimes unstressed short i/u) is never stressed; 'heavy' vowels are full vowels standing alone or heading a vowel sequence; a word contains at most two heavy vowels and stress falls on the first (leftmost) heavy vowel, the second heavy vowel (if any) being word-final and unstressed; inflectional endings are never stressed. Hence stress may surface on the 1st, 2nd or (rarely) 3rd syllable (/ˈsül:e/, /kəˈra:/, /tsəˈlà:p:hər/, /pətshɛ̀ˈk:ərnô/-type patterns in the synopsis p. 40), and Hendriksen marks it only where not inferable. Historically (p. 67) the stressed vowel continues the last non-final MIA long vowel, else the first vowel.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described for simple words; in compound substantives 'each member is stressed separately' (p. 40), the compound forming one rhythmic whole.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics and proclitics are stressless; in Koci (rarely Kotgarhi) single non-final /i/,/u/ and occasionally other vowels may be unstressed and then count as empty vowels (p. 40); derivational stress shift from 1st to 2nd (rarely 3rd) syllable is accompanied by reduction of the destressed vowel to /ə/ and by aspiration shift (pp. 25-26); stress and consonant length 'have a low phonemic status' (p. 10); stress interacts with the two tones (high-falling, high-level), which only the stressed head vowel can bear (p. 44).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word excluding clitics ('Each word which is not enclitic or proclitic has one stress-syllable'); statements are based on field observation and tape recordings of citation forms and texts (1952-53, 1964, 1984); compounds have one stress per member.
new_statements.identity_note: Hendriksen 1986 describes two Upper Mahasu Pahari dialects: Kotgarhi (Ktg., villages Kotgarh/Thanedhar south of the Sutlej, Shimla district; chief object of the grammar) and Koci (Kc., Spail valley c. 2 miles north of Rohru on the Pabar). Both are conventionally listed as Upper Mahasu Pahari dialects (Kotgarhi, Kochi) under bfz/maha1287; Hendriksen himself calls the whole Western Pahari group 'Himachali'. Jouanne 2014 describes Kvari of the Dodra-Kvar (Rupin) valley, which Hendriksen (p. 4) counts among the 'Koci dialects in the wider sense'; Glottolog files the thesis under maha1287, but it borders Bangani/Jaunsari and its affiliation is less secure.

tone_statements.citation: Bailey, T. Grahame. 1920 [t.p. 1915]. Linguistic Studies from the Himalayas, being studies in the grammar of fifteen Himalayan dialects. (Asiatic Society Monographs.) London: Royal Asiatic Society. xv+277 pp. (Preface 'Tones' pp. ix-xii; Kagani 'Pronunciation' pp. 87-89; 'The Koci dialects of Rampur State' pp. 113 ff., tone remark p. 115.)
tone_statements.quote: In the Koci dialects, as in Simla dialects as a whole, sonant letters are not aspirated; thus, the combinations gh, dh, dh, jh, bh are practically unknown, and when they occur they are probably to be put down to Hindi influence. ... The fact, however, is that it is generally omitted altogether, and the only trace of its existence is found in the raising of the tone of the syllable in which one would expect the h. Thus, ... in which words the h is not sounded, the words being, however, pronounced with the high falling tone described under Kagani.
tone_statements.locator: p. 115, 'The Koci dialects of Rampur State: Pronunciation'; cf. Kagani pp. 88-89 and Preface p. x
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: A high falling tone on syllables that historically contained a voiced aspirate or h (h dropped, tone remains), identified with the Kagani/Panjabi high tone ('begins slightly more than half an octave higher than the deep tone, and generally falls about a tone'); the Panjabi-type deep (low-rising) tone is said to be practically absent in the Simla States dialects; tones occur on accented syllables…

sources.note: Compatible with the catalog's Hendriksen 1986 record but adds no placement information; it only confirms that the accented syllable of a Kotgarhi word carries one of two conditioned tones (high falling / high level), which vol. III describes as tones riding on the stressed vowel, not lexical tone. The 1976 volume therefore neither refines nor contradicts the weight-sensitive reading.
